description: The Tauri IPC surface for StackVo Desktop — contract v1. Derived 1:1 from the Express routes in core/ui/server/routes/ and the Socket.io events in core/ui/server/, plus the commands the desktop app needs that no HTTP endpoint ever provided. This file is the agreement between the Vue front end and the Rust core; both sides are generated/checked against it.

conventions.naming: snake_case, <domain>_<verb>. The same string is the Rust #[tauri::command] fn name and the JS invoke() key.

envelope.before: Express returned { success, data?, message?, meta? } and the axios interceptor unwrapped .data — a 200 with success:false was treated as an error.
envelope.after: Tauri commands return Result<T, StackvoError>. Ok(T) is the payload directly (no envelope). Err(e) rejects the invoke() promise. The success:false-with-HTTP-200 ambiguity disappears.
envelope.migration: client/src/lib/api.js is the ONLY file that changes: its interceptor logic becomes a thin invoke() wrapper that re-throws StackvoError as an Error with .code and .hint attached. Pinia stores are untouched.

conventions.argCasing: Rust params are snake_case; Tauri auto-converts camelCase from JS. Send snake_case explicitly to avoid ambiguity.
conventions.longRunning: Any operation that can exceed ~2s (build, compose up, image pull) MUST NOT block on its return value. It returns an OperationId immediately and reports progress via events. This replaces the 600s nginx proxy timeout hack.
conventions.idempotency: start/stop/restart on an already-in-that-state container succeed silently (matches current DockerService behaviour).

codes.ENGINE_UNREACHABLE: Docker daemon not running or socket/pipe not accessible. Replaces the ECONNREFUSED stack spam that isDockerUnreachable() papered over. The UI MUST offer engine_start().
codes.NOT_FOUND: Container, project or service does not exist.
codes.INVALID_INPUT: Failed schema validation. `details` carries the field path.
codes.INVALID_MANIFEST: stackvo.json exists but violates project.schema.json. `details.path` names the offending key.
codes.UNSUPPORTED: Requested runtime/extension/server/platform feature has no implementation in v1 (e.g. runtime=python, extension=pdo_oci, external terminal off macOS).
codes.GENERATE_FAILED: The generator ran and failed. `details.log` carries stderr.
codes.BUILD_FAILED: Docker build returned non-zero. `details.log_path` points at logs/build/<service>.log.
codes.CONFLICT: Port or domain already claimed by another project.
codes.NO_WORKSPACE: No StackVo directory is selected, or the selected one no longer looks like a StackVo checkout. Desktop-only: the web UI could never hit this because it was mounted inside the repo it managed. The UI MUST offer workspace_pick().

errors.policy: No error message may contain a raw shell command line or a value matching the secret redaction regex from env.schema.json.

engine_status.why: There was NO endpoint for this. The web UI could not report a stopped Docker daemon because the UI itself was a container that could not start. This is the single most important new command — it is what makes the desktop app usable when Docker is down.
engine_status.polling: Called on startup and on a 5s timer while disconnected; emits engine:status_changed on transition.

engine_start.why: Launch Docker Desktop (macOS/Windows) or `systemctl --user start docker` (Linux). Resolves the chicken-and-egg problem end to end.
engine_start.notes: Best-effort. Returns Ok as soon as the launch is issued; the caller waits on engine:status_changed.

preflight.why: Everything that has to be true before the app can do anything: a checkout, a reachable daemon, compose v2, the shared network, a projects directory, bash, and mkcert. Without it the app opened regardless and each button failed on its own terms — three different errors, one cause each, none stated up front.
preflight.notes: Runs before the first screen. `Unknown` is a distinct state from failure: with the engine down there is no answer to "does the network exist", and reporting one sends the user after the wrong problem. Declared retroactively — this shipped without a contract entry.

preflight_fix.why: A requirement that reports a problem the app could have fixed itself is a diagnosis pretending to be a product. `fixable` on each Requirement says which ids this accepts.
preflight_fix.notes: Rejects any id it cannot fix rather than silently succeeding — a no-op that returns Ok would report the requirement as repaired on the next poll and it would still be broken. Accepts 'network', 'projects' and 'engine'; the UI reaches engine start through engine_start (it polls for the daemon coming up), the 'engine' arm here is for headless callers. Declared retroactively.

doctor.why: The boot gate answers "can the app run"; this answers the failures that arrive later, one failed compose up at a time. The single most common one — a host port already taken — compose reports as "address already in use" with no word on by what. The doctor names the culprit: the stack's own container (fine), someone else's container (named), or a host process (named, with pid).
doctor.notes: Diagnosis only. Every repair stays behind its own command — preflight_fix, hosts_apply (behind its reviewed diff), generate_run, docker_prune — so no confirmation flow is bypassed. Degrades honestly: no workspace ⇒ port and generated checks read unknown; engine down ⇒ space is null and port owners cannot be named.

docker_disk_usage.why: docker_system_resources reports totals; the question a full disk raises is *which project*. Every StackVo container with its image size and writable layer, plus stack-built images whose container is gone — the bytes nobody remembers spending. No native-binary competitor can ship this at all.
docker_disk_usage.notes: imageDedicated separates images this stack built (stackvo-<name>, freed by removing the member) from shared upstream images (mysql:8.0, freed by nothing short of docker rmi). Sorted largest first.

tunnel_status.why: Webhook testing (Stripe, GitHub) had no answer: myapp.loc does not exist on the internet. This reports every running tunnel sidecar and its assigned public URL.
tunnel_status.notes: The URL is read from the sidecar's own log on every call rather than cached — what the log says is what is actually live, across app restarts and container crashes alike. `url` is null while cloudflared is still connecting; the UI polls until it appears.

tunnel_start.why: Starts a cloudflared quick-tunnel sidecar on the stack's network, forwarding a random trycloudflare.com URL to the project's container. No account, no token — and no host-binary competitor can attach to the container network at all.
tunnel_start.notes: An operation because the first start pulls the cloudflared image, which can take minutes. Targets the project container directly (with the local domain as Host header): with SSL on, every Traefik project router is websecure-only, which a public visitor cannot handshake against. Refuses when the project container is not running — a tunnel serving 502s looks like it worked. The URL that results is public and unauthenticated while the tunnel runs; the UI says so.

tunnel_stop.notes: The sidecar runs with --rm, so stop is also removal — nothing is left behind to leak the old URL.

project_scaffold.why: The create half of P0-1 (detection/adoption shipped first). Runs the framework's own installer in a throwaway container — composer create-project, wp-cli, create-next-app — so nothing is installed on the host and only the bind-mounted project directory survives.
project_scaffold.notes: Ends where adoption begins: the UI follows with project_adopt, which detects runtime/server/document root from what the installer actually wrote — the same machinery as a git clone. Nine installers, every command pinned non-interactive — each flag measured against a real container rather than read off a README (nuxi needs both --template and --force; sv needs --no-add-ons; astro needs --yes). The JavaScript ones pass --no-install: the node Dockerfile installs for the container's platform, and a host node_modules in the image is the arm64-in-amd64 mistake NODE_DOCKERIGNORE exists to prevent (a prompt inside an operation console is a hang, not a question). On unix runs --user uid:gid so files land owned by the user, not root. Refuses a non-empty directory; a failed install that wrote nothing removes the husk so the retry is not blocked. Seventeen installers now, across PHP, JavaScript, Python and Ruby. Composer projects carry --ignore-platform-reqs because the installer container is not the machine the code runs on (CakePHP wants ext-intl, the composer image has none, and StackVo's PHP image does); Rails needs the full ruby image rather than slim, which cannot compile websocket-driver. Twenty-eight templates in two kinds: an installer container where the ecosystem has a scaffolder, and **written files** where it does not — Gin, Echo, Flask, FastAPI, Sinatra and Rocket are each 'write two files and let the language build them', so pulling an image to write thirty lines would be a download for nothing. Their dependencies are not skipped, they move: the project's own Dockerfile already runs pip/go build/bundle/cargo for the container's platform. Every written template binds 0.0.0.0 on the port lang_defaults gives its runtime — a test asserts it over code lines only, because the comments explaining the loopback trap were tripping the check.

worker_options.why: Which workers this project can offer, from its files alone: artisan offers 'queue' and 'scheduler', laravel/horizon in composer.json adds 'horizon'. A Node project gets an empty list, not an error.

worker_status.why: A Laravel app runs queue:work, the scheduler and Horizon beside the web server; locally they live in a forgotten terminal tab, which is why "my job never ran" is a support staple. This reports every worker sidecar with its restart count — the self-heal made visible; a large number is a crash loop, not a success story.

worker_start.notes: The sidecar runs the project's own image (same PHP, extensions, bind mount and network, so .env and the database resolve as the web container sees them) with --restart unless-stopped — self-healing is Docker's own supervisor, not reimplemented. queue:work carries --max-time=3600 on purpose: a worker holds the code it booted with, and an hour caps how long it serves yesterday's code. Refuses when the project has no built container.

worker_stop.notes: Removal, not just stop: with unless-stopped, a merely-stopped container is one engine restart away from coming back.

docker_prune.why: SystemResources has reported reclaimable bytes since Phase 1 with no way to act on the number. Dangling images accumulate on every rebuild, and this app rebuilds a lot — every Xdebug toggle, every extension change.
docker_prune.notes: Images means dangling images only (the engine's default prune set — rebuildable by definition). Volumes are a separate flag because the engine's "unused" means "not currently mounted", and the database of a stopped project qualifies; the UI warns before passing volumes:true. Guarded by the 'prune' inflight subject.

workspace_get.why: The web UI never needed this — it ran inside the StackVo repo, so its root was `/app` by mount. A desktop app has to be told, or work it out. Returns the resolved root plus how it was resolved, so the UI can show the user which checkout it is driving.

workspace_set.notes: Validates that the path contains core/cli/stackvo.sh and projects/ before accepting it, then persists it. Rejects with NO_WORKSPACE and an explanation rather than silently accepting a wrong folder.

workspace_pick.notes: Opens the native directory picker, then applies workspace_set. Returns null if the user cancels.

project_get.why: ProjectDetail.vue currently re-fetches the whole list and filters client-side.

project_validate.why: Pre-flight the new-project form against project.schema.json + php-extensions.json before anything touches disk. Today a bad extension name is only discovered when the Docker build fails minutes later.

project_create.notes: Writes the manifest, runs generate, then builds. The build half is what makes it an operation rather than a mutation.

project_delete.notes: remove_files is NEW and MUST default to false. The current deleteProject() removes the project directory outright with no confirmation contract — a desktop app deleting user source code needs an explicit opt-in.

project_manifest_write.why: Editing an existing project is impossible today — the UI can only create and delete. MUST honour the write rules in project.schema.json (extensions last, one runtime block).

service_enable.notes: Flips SERVICE_<NAME>_ENABLE in .env, regenerates, then brings the profile up.

service_settings.replaces: none — new in the desktop app
service_settings.notes: Every SERVICE_<ID>_* key except ENABLE, which the services list owns. Secrets are masked; env_reveal is the only way to see one.

service_apply_settings.replaces: none — new in the desktop app
service_apply_settings.notes: MUST reject keys outside the service's prefix, MUST reject ENABLE, and MUST reject a masked value being written back. Regenerates and recreates the container: a restart would keep the environment it was created with, so the setting would appear applied and not be.

service_dependencies.notes: Kept for completeness; services_list already returns required/optional/unmetDependencies per service, so the front end has no reason to call this separately.

host_stats.v1Change: Backed by the `sysinfo` crate on the host instead of reading /proc from inside a container. The 293-line HostStatsService with its macOS fallbacks collapses to a direct, correct read — this is the clearest early win of the port.

container_stats_history.notes: Sampler runs at 60s (startStatsSampler). v1 MUST persist history across app restarts — today it lives in memory and dies with the container.

container_logs_open.why: Log following existed only as `stackvo logs` in the CLI. The UI had no way to tail a container.

app_logs.why: The container stream carries stdout and stderr, which is what the entrypoint and the web server say — not what the application records. A Laravel exception goes to storage/logs/laravel.log, an nginx 502 to the mounted error.log, and a queue worker that died to its own file under supervisord. None of those reach stdout, so none of them were visible anywhere in the app.
app_logs.notes: Reads the host filesystem, not the container: the generated compose mounts projects/<name> at /var/www/html and logs/projects/<name> at /var/log, so both roots are already there. No engine required — which is the point, because a container that crashed on boot is exactly when its log is worth reading and exactly when there is nothing left to exec into. Discovery recurses, because Laravel channels nest (storage/logs/parser/parser-2026-07-28.log is a real path from the checkout this was built against), and is capped at depth 3 and 60 files so a stray node_modules cannot turn it into a full-disk walk.

app_log_open.why: Follows one of those files. Shares the event pair with container_logs_open because the viewer renders one kind of line; a second pair would have meant a second frontend listener free to drift from the first. Closed with container_logs_close — one registry of abort handles, one way to stop a stream.
app_log_open.notes: `id` is an opaque `app:` or `server:` handle from app_logs, never a path. Paths do not cross the boundary in either direction: a log viewer that accepts an absolute path from its own frontend is a file reader for the whole disk. The id's components are checked for traversal before the filesystem is touched, and the resolved path is checked against its root again afterwards, because a symlink inside the project can escape with no `..` in sight. Polled twice a second rather than watched — a notification still only says that something changed, so the read-the-delta path exists either way. A file shorter than the reader's offset was truncated or rotated (`> laravel.log`, or a daily channel rolling over) and restarts from the top instead of going silent for ever.

app_logs_all.why: The per-project viewer answers "what did this project write". It cannot answer "which of my eight projects just errored", which is the question you have when you do not yet know where to look. Herd sells the cross-project view as a Pro feature.
app_logs_all.notes: A project is a directory under projects/ holding a stackvo.json — an unadopted checkout is somebody's folder, not something this app follows. No engine is consulted anywhere on this path, so with Docker stopped this is the one list in the app that is still complete.

app_logs_all_open.why: One live tail across every project, so an error surfaces without first guessing which project to open.
app_logs_all_open.returnsNote: Returns the first scan's coverage rather than emitting it. An event would race the caller — the spawned task can emit before the frontend holds the stream id it filters events by, and the coverage line would then stay blank until the next rediscovery thirty seconds later. logs:sources carries updates only, because only an update has somewhere to arrive.
app_logs_all_open.notes: **Live only, with no history — a decision, not an omission.** Nothing in this module parses a timestamp (Laravel, nginx and supervisord do not agree on a format), so the only chronology available across sixty files is the order bytes arrive in: real for new output, invented for old. Each file is therefore adopted at its current end and only what follows is shown; history stays in app_log_open, which reads one file and can honestly show all of it. Rediscovery every 30s is the other half — a daily channel rolls over into a filename that did not exist when the tail started, so a fixed file set would go quiet exactly at midnight. Files found by a later scan are adopted at offset zero, because everything in a file that new was written while the tail was already watching. Capped at 60 files, newest first, with what was dropped reported through logs:sources rather than trimmed silently. Closed with container_logs_close — one registry of abort handles, one way to stop a stream.

env_get.notes: MUST redact secret-matching keys unless `reveal: true` is passed and the user has confirmed in-session.

server_config_get.replaces: none — new in the desktop app
server_config_get.notes: The raw file including its comments. Only nginx and caddy are accepted; the other servers have no generated config file for a snippet to be added to.

server_config_set.replaces: none — new in the desktop app
server_config_set.notes: Written atomically. Takes effect on the next generate: the directives are rendered into each project's server config, not into a file the server reads directly.

env_defaults.replaces: none — new in the desktop app
env_defaults.notes: The values compiled into the binary. Carries no secret and needs no workspace: it describes the app, not a checkout. The settings form uses it to mark a value as a default and to offer going back to one.

env_reveal.why: env_get redacts secrets, so revealing one needs a separate call the user has to ask for. Returning the whole map unmasked on a flag would put every password in one payload the moment anyone wanted to see one.
env_reveal.notes: One key per call, by design. Declared retroactively: this shipped in lib.rs without a contract entry and suite E was reporting it as UNDECLARED_COMMAND.

env_set.why: Settings.vue is a 24-line stub because .env was read-only over HTTP. Writing MUST preserve comments, key order and blank lines — a naive rewrite destroys a 159-key hand-annotated file.

catalog_get.v1Change: Served from the bundled contracts (php-extensions.json + env.schema.json), no longer re-parsed out of .env on every request. Runtimes without generators are marked available:false rather than silently offered.

generate_run.why: `stackvo generate` was only ever invoked as a side effect of project_create / service_enable, via execAsync on a shell string. Making it a first-class command is what lets the fs-watcher regenerate automatically.
generate_run.notes: Since the takeover, this writes with the Rust generator directly — no shell is spawned, and bash is no longer a generation prerequisite.

compose_down.why: `stackvo down` existed only in the CLI — the web UI could never stop the stack, because doing so would have killed the UI itself.

pty_open.v1Change: PtyTarget is NEW: { kind: 'container', name } or { kind: 'host', cwd }. node-pty could only reach containers because it ran inside one; portable-pty on the host can open a real host shell in the project directory.

terminal_open_external.v1Change: Always works. The HTTP version returned HTTP 400 with 'Terminal cannot be opened from containerized environment' — it could never succeed in the shipped configuration.

hosts_status.why: readHostsFile() could only READ a read-only mount and report isDomainConfigured. Same capability, but now it feeds a fix action.
hosts_status.notes: Rust-internal: projects_list uses it to fill `domainConfigured`. Deliberately not wrapped for JS — the list payload already carries the answer, and a second round trip is a way for the two to disagree.

hosts_apply.why: Removes the manual `sudo tee -a /etc/hosts` step from the README. MUST show a diff and require explicit confirmation before elevating; MUST back up the file; MUST only touch lines inside a StackVo-managed marker block.
hosts_apply.notes: Writes the previewed text via the OS elevation prompt (osascript / pkexec / UAC). Only lines inside the `# >>> stackvo >>>` marker block are rewritten; everything else in the file is byte-identical. A cancelled prompt is PERMISSION_DENIED, not a crash.

open_path.notes: Implemented in the front end via the opener plugin rather than as a Rust command: the plugin already does exactly this, and wrapping it would add a hop with no behaviour of its own. The capability is allow-listed in capabilities/default.json.

open_url.notes: Same as open_path. The plugin restricts schemes; the allow-list in capabilities/default.json is the control point.

open_in_editor.notes: Editor command from preferences; default: detect VS Code, fall back to the OS handler.

open_in_browser.why: A project's own domain deserves the browser the developer works in, not whatever the OS last associated with https. The opener plugin has no notion of which browser.
open_in_browser.notes: Also the fix for a real defect: `opener:allow-open-url` was granted without a scope, and open_url answers ForbiddenUrl when nothing matches — so every visit button in the app did nothing at all, silently. http/https only; a launcher that took file:// or a custom scheme from its own front end would be a way to start arbitrary things. Falls back to the system default when the chosen browser cannot start.

open_folder.replaces: none — new in the desktop app
open_folder.notes: Shows a directory in the system file manager. Its own command rather than the opener plugin's open_path, whose permission is documented as enabling the command with no scope — and a scope wide enough for an arbitrary workspace is a scope over everything. MUST reject a path that is not an existing directory.

pick_directory.why: Adopting an existing folder as a project is impossible today; paths are typed by hand.
pick_directory.notes: Used directly by the front end. `workspace_pick` is the Rust command that matters, because it pairs the picker with validation and persistence.

apps_available.notes: Terminals and editors present on this machine, each with { id, name, icon, available }. Entries that are not installed are returned with available:false rather than omitted, so the picker can grey them out — a list that silently drops them reads as lack of support.

window_close_action.notes: Carries out the choice the close dialog collected, optionally storing it as closeBehaviour. Four behaviours exist including "ask"; the extra "quit" (close, leave the stack running) is meaningful here because the containers are Docker's and outlive the app.

tray_relabel.notes: Re-label the tray menu after the user changes language. The tray is built natively and has six strings of its own; without this it keeps the language it was built with until the next launch.

logs_info.returns: { directory: string|null, newestFile: string|null, totalBytes: number }
logs_info.notes: Where the diagnostic log lives. New to the desktop app — the container UI wrote to stdout, which docker logs captured and nobody kept. The path differs per platform (~/Library/Logs on macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA% on Windows, ~/.local/share on Linux) and none is somewhere a user would look unprompted.

updater_status.returns: { configured: boolean, hasPublicKey: boolean, endpoints: number }
updater_status.notes: Whether this build can verify an update. Tauri checks a bundle's signature against the public key compiled into the app; with an empty `pubkey` every check fails inside the plugin with a message about signatures, which reads like a server fault and is a build fault. Read from tauri.conf.json via include_str! so the answer describes the binary, not the working tree.

system_accent.returns: { available: boolean, name: string|null, hex: string|null }
system_accent.why: The desktop's own accent colour, so the app can match it instead of shipping a brand colour that clashes with everyone's system theme.
system_accent.notes: macOS reads AppleHighlightColor via `defaults` and maps it to the eight colours the OS itself draws with. Elsewhere `available` is false and both fields are null — Windows keeps its accent in the registry, and saying "unknown" beats returning a wrong blue. Declared retroactively — this shipped without a contract entry.

prefs_get.notes: Replaces the localStorage-backed usePreferences composable with the Tauri store plugin.

updates_check.notes: Needs tauri-plugin-updater plus a signing key and a release endpoint — i.e. a release pipeline, not just code. Deferred to Phase 4 alongside signed builds. Declared here so the surface is complete and the gap is visible.

hosts_plan.why: Computes the exact replacement text WITHOUT elevating, so the UI can show a diff and ask first. Elevating and explaining afterwards would be the wrong order for the one operation that touches a system file.

hosts_missing.why: Every project domain with no hosts entry. Drives the one-click fix; the web UI could detect this but had no way to act on it.

hosts_overview.replaces: none — new in the desktop app
hosts_overview.notes: Every domain the stack serves with its hosts state, plus entries inside StackVo's own block that nothing wants any more. MUST offer only StackVo-managed lines as stale: a hand-written entry belongs to whoever wrote it.

cert_status.why: HTTPS was already working and entirely invisible. `core/cli/utils/generate-ssl-certs.sh` issues an mkcert wildcard covering stackvo.loc and every project domain, and traefik.sh installs it as the default certificate — but nothing in the app could say whether mkcert was installed, whether the CA was trusted, whether the certificate had expired, or which domains it actually covered. A user whose new project shows a browser warning had no way to learn why.
cert_status.notes: Reads only: it never runs mkcert and never writes. The SAN list and expiry are parsed out of the certificate itself rather than inferred from the project list, because the file on disk is what the browser validates against — a list of what SHOULD be covered would agree with the certificate right up until it mattered.

cert_plan.why: Same order as hosts_plan: say what would change before doing it. Reissuing replaces the file Traefik is serving, and `installCa` can touch the system trust store, so neither should be the first thing the user learns about it.
cert_plan.notes: `domains` is the exact argument list mkcert would be invoked with — the same value cert_apply uses, not a second computation that could differ.

cert_apply.why: Reissues the wildcard certificate for the domains the projects actually have, and — when the CA is not trusted yet — installs it. Without this the certificate goes stale the moment a project is created, and on Linux and Windows the CA is never trusted at all: the Bash helper's trust step returns early on anything but macOS, so those users get a browser warning and no explanation.
cert_apply.notes: Trust installation delegates to `mkcert -install` rather than reimplementing four trust stores (macOS keychain, Linux ca-certificates, NSS for Firefox and Chrome, Windows Root). mkcert may need a password for the system store; on Linux it shells out to sudo, which a GUI process has no terminal for. That failure MUST be reported with the exact command to run, not swallowed — a CA that silently failed to install looks identical to one that worked until the browser disagrees. Issuing the certificate itself writes only inside the workspace and never elevates.

project_adoptable.why: `project_create` refuses when the directory already exists, so a folder cloned into projects/ could not be brought under management at all — the only way in was writing stackvo.json by hand. On the checkout this was written against, 11 of 21 directories under projects/ were in that state: real code, unmanaged.
project_adoptable.notes: Reads only, and needs no Docker. Each entry carries a detected runtime, server, document root and framework, plus the files that detection was based on — a document root inferred wrongly produces a project that builds, starts and serves a 404, which is a failure with no error attached to it.

args.name: string
args.spec: ProjectSpec (optional — defaults to what was detected)
args.domain: string? — overrides the detected domain only

project_adopt.why: Writes stackvo.json for a directory that is already there, then regenerates. The counterpart of project_create, which requires the directory to be absent.
project_adopt.notes: Refuses when a manifest already exists — adopting a managed project would silently overwrite settings the user chose. The spec is validated against project.schema.json exactly as project_create's is; detection fills the form, it does not bypass the check. `domain` is an override on top of detection rather than part of the spec: detection reads the code and can say "this is Laravel, its document root is public", but it has no way to know the user wanted `shop.loc` instead of `<directory>.loc`. Passing a full spec still bypasses detection entirely; passing only a domain does not.

mail_status.why: StackVo has shipped a mail catcher all along and never showed it — reading a captured message meant leaving for a browser tab, which is exactly the round trip four competitors charge for removing.
mail_status.notes: Reads both MailHog and Mailpit. The upstream template installs the unmaintained `mailhog/mailhog`; Mailpit is what the ecosystem moved to, and swapping renames a service, its .env keys, its container and its volume — a migration for every running stack. Supporting both is the same stance the app takes everywhere else: it manages a checkout, it does not dictate one. `error` is set when the container is up but its API did not answer, because that otherwise renders as an empty inbox, which is a lie.

mail_messages.notes: Both wire formats are normalised in Rust. They agree on almost nothing: MailHog spells an address as `{Mailbox, Domain}` and buries the subject in a header array, Mailpit uses `{Name, Address}` and a field. Reading either as the other yields an inbox of blank rows that still look like messages.

mail_message.notes: Mailpit returns decoded text and HTML parts. MailHog returns the raw MIME document and leaves decoding to the caller, so `html` is always null there — showing a half-decoded multipart as if it were the message would be worse than showing the source.

mail_clear.notes: DESTRUCTIVE in the small: it empties the inbox. The UI MUST confirm, but this needs no backup — a mail catcher is a bin by design.

mail_delete.notes: One message, not the inbox. The servers disagree on the verb's address: MailHog takes the id in the path, Mailpit takes a JSON body of ids on the collection route. No confirmation — a catcher is a bin; only the whole-inbox clear keeps its dialog.

mail_search.why: A catcher with fifty captured mails needs a search box more than it needs another button. The query reaches the catcher verbatim, so Mailpit's own syntax (from:, to:, subject:, quoted phrases) works as documented rather than being reimplemented worse here.

mail_html_check.why: The report a developer actually opens a catcher for: how this markup fares across 186 real mail-client features. Mailpit only — null on MailHog, which is how the UI knows to hide the tab instead of showing zeroes.
mail_html_check.notes: Warnings are sorted worst-first; a report whose first row is a construct every client supports buries the one that breaks Outlook.

mail_link_check.why: Dead links in a transactional mail are found by the recipient today.
mail_link_check.notes: **This leaves the machine** — it fetches every link in the message, so it is never run as part of opening one; the UI asks for it explicitly. 30s timeout, because it waits on third-party servers.

mail_attachment_save.why: Reading a captured invoice PDF meant leaving for the browser UI.
mail_attachment_save.notes: partId is a handle the catcher issued and path comes from the system save dialog — the front end names neither the source nor the destination.

db_targets.why: Which database services can be dumped, what they are called, and whether they are running. The credentials were already read out of .env and rendered in the services list; what was missing was anything to do with them.
db_targets.notes: Reads .env and the engine. A service that is enabled but not running is still listed, with `running: false` — the reason a dump cannot start right now is worth showing next to the button that is disabled because of it.

db_dump.why: Lerd sells snapshots, Laragon sells automatic backups, ServBay sells both; StackVo had no way to take a copy of a database at all. The tools are already inside the container — `mysqldump`, `pg_dump` and `mongodump` ship with the images the stack runs.
db_dump.notes: Streams the dump straight from `docker exec` into the chosen file rather than buffering it: a production-sized database does not fit in a UI process's memory, and the failure would arrive as an out-of-memory kill with no explanation. The password is passed through the child's environment and named — not valued — on the docker command line, so it does not appear in `ps` output on a shared machine.

db_restore.why: A backup nobody has restored is a file, not a backup.
db_restore.notes: DESTRUCTIVE: this replaces the contents of the target database. The UI MUST name the database and require confirmation before calling it. Reads the file into the container's stdin, the mirror of how the dump was written.

xdebug_status.why: Step debugging is the thing Docker makes hardest and the thing a PHP developer needs most. `xdebug` was already in the extension catalog with per-version pecl pins, so it could be compiled in by hand-editing stackvo.json — and then it still would not connect, because nothing set xdebug.mode or told it which host the IDE is on. This reports all three layers separately: listed in the manifest, present in the built image, and live in the running container.
xdebug_status.notes: `active` is read from the running container's environment rather than assumed from the manifest. The two disagree in a case users hit: `stackvo up` from the CLI does not layer the overlay this app writes, so it recreates the container without the Xdebug environment and debugging stops working with nothing on screen to explain it.

xdebug_set.why: One switch instead of three manual steps: adding the extension to the manifest, configuring the client host and port, and telling the IDE where the code is mounted.
xdebug_set.notes: Writes `php.extensions` in the manifest and re-renders `generated/docker-compose.xdebug.yml`. The extension is COMPILED IN, so enabling it needs a rebuild before it takes effect — `needsRebuild` says so rather than letting the toggle look finished. Writing the manifest canonicalises it the same way project_manifest_write does (`webserver` becomes `server`); that is the contract's rule for writers, not a side effect of this command.

doctor_drop_extension.why: The doctor's design rule is a repair next to every finding — hosts get the reviewed diff, stale output gets regenerate, disk gets prune. The extension check shipped without one, which left the panel naming a problem and offering nothing.
doctor_drop_extension.notes: **Removing the extension changes nothing about what runs, and that is the point.** The generator already drops one it cannot install — silently, which is the bug CONFLICTS.md C-06 records — so it is already absent from every built container. This does not remove a capability; it stops the manifest claiming one the container never had. No alternative is offered because the catalog leaves none: `imap` is `install: core` with `removedIn: 8.2` and no PECL package, so on 8.2+ there is nothing StackVo could install instead. If the project genuinely needs it the answer is an older PHP version, which is the project owner's decision and not a button. Writes through the paths the rest of the app uses — manifest::write for a project, env_writer for .env, which backs the file up and serialises against the other writers. Removing an extension that is already gone is a no-op rather than an error: the state the caller wanted is the state on disk.

dumps_status.why: P3-18 was rated expensive on the grounds that it "needs a collector service and a Composer package". Checked against real projects, neither half holds for Laravel: symfony/var-dumper is a laravel/framework dependency and is present in every checkout here that has a vendor/ at all, and `vendor/bin/var-dump-server` — the collector — ships with it.
dumps_status.notes: What IS expensive is the thing that looks obvious: writing the collector. VAR_DUMPER_FORMAT=server sends base64(serialize([Data, context])) over a socket — a PHP object graph. Reading that in Rust means a serialize() parser PLUS Symfony's internal Cloner\Data representation, where a nested value is an indirection into a per-depth slot table and every object is a Stub. That is a lot of code sitting on an internal Symfony is free to change, and the failure mode when it does is a viewer that renders nonsense. So the collector is not written: Symfony's own runs inside the project container and renders the dumps itself, and this app streams the text. `available` is false when the vendor tree has no collector — usually a checkout whose dependencies were never installed. `configured` is read from the RUNNING container, not inferred, because `stackvo up` from the Bash CLI layers three compose files and will recreate it without the variables.

dumps_open.notes: Reuses the log stream's events and its close command on purpose: the viewer already renders one kind of line, and a second event pair would be a second listener that could drift from the first. `source` is `dumps`. The server's four-line opening banner is filtered — in a pane whose whole job is to show dumps it would be the first thing on screen and the only thing there until somebody dumped something. Started with `docker exec -w /var/www/html` and NO `-t`: the process is driven by the app, not a person, and `docker exec -t` without a TTY fails on the input device. Aborting the task drops the child, and kill_on_drop stops the collector with it.

dumps_close.why: **Killing `docker exec` does not kill what it exec'd.** The client goes away; the PHP collector inside the container keeps running and keeps port 9912. The next dumps_open then fails with Symfony's own `stream_socket_server(): Address already in use` — which is exactly how this was found, by the integration test failing its second run.
dumps_close.notes: This is why dumps do NOT close through container_logs_close like every other stream: aborting the task is only half of it. The same `pkill` also runs inside dumps_open's prepare step, so a collector left behind by a crash — or by a `docker exec` that died with the app — does not block the next attempt. Self-healing beats depending on a clean shutdown that cannot be guaranteed. Verified by running the integration test twice back to back, which is the case that used to fail, and by confirming no `var-dump-server` process survives in any container afterwards.

release_plan.why: P3-20 — what `laradock ship` does. The analysis calls it the long-horizon differentiator because the container lineage makes it possible and no native-binary competitor can follow. It is also the item with a real question inside it, answered by looking at what the images actually contain rather than by assuming.
release_plan.notes: **The dev image is not a production image**, measured on this checkout: a PHP project's image holds NO application code — /var/www/html contains one file, index.nginx-debian.html, because the source arrives through a bind mount — and it has Xdebug loaded. Exporting it ships a web server with nothing to serve and a step debugger that dials out on every request. A NODE image is the opposite: its Dockerfile does COPY . . and npm install, so it already holds the code and the build. Hence two strategies: `layer` (build FROM the dev image, add the source, remove the debugger inis) and `retag` (nothing to add; rebuilding would replace a Linux node_modules with whatever the host has). `excluded` carries every ignore pattern WITH ITS REASON, because an exclusion the user cannot explain is one they work around. `warnings` names what the result will be true of — no .env, vendor as it is on disk, Xdebug's binary still present though inactive — before the build rather than after.

release_build.notes: **Verification is not optional and not a separate button.** The safety property here — no .env in the image, no active debugger — is exactly the kind that is easy to state in a Dockerfile and quietly wrong in the result, so the built image is RUN and asked. Proven both ways on a real project: with the ignore file, zero env files; without it, all five of that project's .env.* land in a layer and the check names every one. `hasApp` catches the other silent failure — a build whose context was empty produces an image that starts and serves nothing, which otherwise looks like a success. The ignore file is written BESIDE the generated Dockerfile as `Dockerfile.dockerignore`, which BuildKit reads in preference to the context's — confirmed to work before anything depended on it — so building somebody's image writes nothing into their repository. The tag is validated before it reaches a command line: lowercase only, because Docker rejects an uppercase repository with an error that does not say so.

release_save.notes: `docker save` to a tarball — the artefact you hand to something that is not this machine.

profiler_status.why: P3-17 named Blackfire and SPX, and both are the wrong door. Blackfire ships a template already and needs an ACCOUNT — a signup wall in a local development tool. SPX, XHProf and Excimer are not in contracts/php-extensions.json (only xdebug is), so adding one is a change to a contract shared with upstream, the same class of decision as the Mailpit swap. **Xdebug is already a profiler**: xdebug.mode=profile writes cachegrind files, the extension is in the catalog, and the overlay that sets XDEBUG_MODE already belongs to this app. That is the one route with no contract change attached.
profiler_status.notes: Profiling is a MODE of the existing Xdebug toggle, not a second switch — the extension has to be compiled in either way, and two switches for one extension is two states to explain instead of one. The mode is `debug` or `profile`, never both: they want opposite start triggers (stepping wants to connect on the next request, profiling wants a trigger so an idle stack does not write a multi-megabyte file per page load), so a combined mode would have to break one of them. `trigger` is the name a request must carry — XDEBUG_TRIGGER as a cookie, GET, POST or environment value.

profiler_set_mode.notes: Stored in `projects/<name>/.stackvo/xdebug.json`, beside php.ini and devserver.json, for the same two reasons: the manifest schema is additionalProperties:false, and a file under .stackvo/ travels with a clone. On/off stays in `php.extensions`, because that is what compiles the extension in. Switching to `profile` writes `generated/xdebug/<name>.ini` and mounts it read-only at /usr/local/etc/php/conf.d/zzz-stackvo-xdebug.ini. **Why an ini and not the environment**: measured against a running container, XDEBUG_CONFIG does carry `output_dir` and `start_with_request` — both took effect — but it silently ignores `use_compression`, and Xdebug 3.4 gzips by default. One compressed file is the difference between a profile view and a parse error. `zzz-` rather than `zz-` because zz-stackvo.ini is the USER's php.ini from php_ini_set; a name sorting before it would let a hand-written xdebug.output_dir send profiles somewhere this app cannot read, which presents as profiling that produced nothing. The mode itself stays in XDEBUG_MODE and is deliberately absent from the ini: the environment variable takes precedence over xdebug.mode, so setting both invites them to disagree.

profiler_read.notes: Cachegrind, read off real Xdebug 3.4.0 output rather than from a specification. Four properties decide the parser. (1) Names are COMPRESSED and the ids are NOT in order — a real file defined fl=(2) before fl=(1), and cfn=(n) can reference a name defined further down, so names are resolved at the end; resolving as you read produces blanks. (2) Every call gets its own block: a 200,000-iteration loop produced **200,004 fn= blocks across 1.6 million lines**, so aggregating by name is not a nicety. (3) A cost line's meaning depends on what preceded it — after fn= it is SELF cost, after calls= it is the INCLUSIVE cost of that call, attributed to the callee. Getting that wrong doubles every caller's self time and is invisible in the output. (4) Units are declared in the file (`events: Time_(10ns) Memory_(bytes)`), not fixed — assuming microseconds would be wrong by two orders of magnitude on this build. `percent` is a share of `selfTotal`, not of the file's `summary`: that denominator is the one that makes "how much of the work happened in here" true and adds to 100. A gzipped file is REFUSED with an explanation rather than parsed into nonsense. Capped at 256 MB with `truncated` reported, because a truncated profile with no warning is a performance conclusion drawn from half the data.

profiler_delete.notes: `id` is a bare `cachegrind.out.*` file name, checked before it is joined to a path — the same handle-not-a-path rule app_log_open runs on.

profiler_clear.why: Profiling fills a disk fast — the 200,000-iteration loop that shaped the parser produced a 10 MB file from one run — so "clear these" has to be one button, not sixty.

quick_commands.why: P3-19 was "a tinker quick action — the PTY exists, so it is nearly free". It is, and on its own it is also one button. What is worth building is the set it belongs to: artisan tinker, artisan migrate, composer install, npm install, wp shell. Each of those today means opening a terminal, remembering the container name and typing `docker exec -it stackvo-<project> …`.
quick_commands.notes: Offered only when the marker file exists — driven off the same Fingerprint adoption uses, so "does this project have artisan" is answered in one place. Offering a command the project cannot run is worse than omitting it: the failure arrives as `artisan: not found` in an operation console, which reads as a broken app rather than as a button that never applied. `because` names the file the offer is based on. Deliberately ABSENT: migrate:fresh, migrate:reset, db:wipe and composer update — the first three drop the user's data behind a button four characters from the safe one, and the last rewrites a lock file. Those are things to type deliberately in the terminal that is one click away.

quick_command_run.notes: **The fixed catalog is the security model.** The frontend sends an ID, never a command; the argv is built on the Rust side from compiled-in words, so there is no code path by which the webview can name a program to execute — the same handle-not-a-path rule app_log_open uses, for the same reason: a project pane that accepted an arbitrary command string from its own frontend is a remote shell with extra steps. Every command is spawned as an argv ARRAY, never through a shell, so a project called `a; rm -rf ~` is a container name that does not exist rather than a second command. Two kinds, because they behave differently: interactive commands (tinker, wp shell) need a TTY and a human, so they open the user's own terminal and return null — an in-app REPL would be a second, worse one next to the one they have configured; one-shot commands stream through the operation console. `-it` is added only for the interactive ones, because Docker refuses `-t` when stdin is not a TTY. Refuses when the container is not running, so the failure is "the project is not running" rather than Docker's "No such container".

devserver_status.why: P2-15 was written as "proxy the Node dev server through Traefik with HMR", which sounds like a routing change. Reading node.sh against the other five server generators turns up something larger: **a node project has no bind mount at all**. nginx/caddy/apache/swoole/frankenphp all call generate_common_volumes; node.sh calls nothing, and its Dockerfile does `COPY . .` and `RUN npm install` at build time. The container holds a SNAPSHOT of the source. Hot reload was not misconfigured — it was structurally impossible, and no amount of WebSocket plumbing helps when there is nothing to reload.
devserver_status.notes: Three things have to be true at once, reported separately because they come apart and each has a different fix. (1) The source is live — a bind over /app plus an ANONYMOUS VOLUME on /app/node_modules, without which the bind shadows the install the image did for its own platform, or worse, exposes the host's macOS build of the same native packages. (2) The dev server is what is running — `npm run dev`, not the manifest's production start command. Both are the overlay's job. (3) The dev server accepts the request, and that one is in the USER'S repository. Read out of Vite's own source (hostValidationMiddleware, verified against the copy in this repo's node_modules): a Host header that is not localhost, not *.localhost, not an IP and not matched by server.allowedHosts gets a flat 403 — so a .loc domain presents as a site that is plainly up and returns 403, with nothing pointing at the dev server's config. The HMR client is the second half: StackVo's node router is websecure-only with tls=true, so the page loads over 443 while the dev server listens on 3000, and Vite's client would dial wss://domain:3000, which nothing routes, and degrade silently to full reloads. `snippet` is the exact config with the project's domain already in it. It is GENERATED, NEVER WRITTEN: silently rewriting somebody's build config is not a thing a local environment manager should do, and a snippet they paste is one they have read.

args.name: string
args.command: string? (defaults to the detected npm script)

devserver_set.notes: State is `projects/<name>/.stackvo/devserver.json` — a file rather than a manifest key, because the manifest schema is additionalProperties:false and because a file under .stackvo/ is commit-friendly: a teammate's clone gets dev mode with everything else. Its existence is the switch; its contents are the command. Node only; a PHP project is refused, and the overlay renderer refuses again for a config file dropped in by hand, since /app does not exist there and mounting over it would replace the site with an empty directory. The overlay is layered LAST of the six compose files, because it is the only one that overrides rather than adds — anything after it would merge onto a service already in a different mode.

migrate_scan.why: The other half of P2-12. The folder half shipped with adoption in Sprint 4 — detection infers runtime, server and document root from artisan/wp-config.php/composer.json. What it cannot see is everything the person who wrote the compose file already decided: the PHP version, the domain, the extensions, and — with no equivalent in any marker file — WHICH BACKING SERVICES the project needs. A compose file with mysql:8.0 and redis:7.2 is a statement about the stack; adoption alone leaves the developer to rediscover it from a stack trace about a refused connection.
migrate_scan.notes: **Docker parses the YAML, not this app.** `docker compose config --format json` is the reference implementation of the Compose spec: it resolves anchors, `extends`, .env interpolation and profiles, and normalises every shorthand (a label list becomes a map, "8080:80" becomes a structured port, a relative bind becomes an absolute path). The alternative was a YAML crate, and that was the wrong trade twice: serde_yaml is archived, and deny.toml here says a DIRECT dependency going unmaintained still fails the build; and a hand parser would be wrong on real files — xdebug::generated_services parses by indentation only because it reads a file this project generated, whose shape is fixed. Compose is already a hard preflight requirement, so this adds no dependency at all; when it is missing the answer is an error, not a half-parse. Three kinds of compose service are told apart because they become three different things: the one with a `build:` (or a php/node image) is the APPLICATION and becomes the manifest; nginx/apache/caddy become the manifest's `server` field and NOT a StackVo service, because StackVo runs the web server inside the project container and importing it as a sidecar would give the project two; everything in the catalog becomes a service to enable. Anything else is NAMED in `unmapped`, never dropped — a migration that silently ignores the one service the project actually needs is worse than one that refuses, because it looks finished. Reading only; the reply's `spec` is already validated against project.schema.json, because reviewing a spec that would then be refused is a review of nothing.

migrate_apply.notes: Adopts first, enables services second, and the order is load-bearing: adoption is the half that can fail on a schema violation, and enabling services for a project that then did not get created leaves the stack carrying a database nothing uses. Skips adoption when the directory already has a manifest, so re-running it against a managed project only reconciles the services. Re-scans afterwards, so the reply describes the state that now exists rather than the one that did before the write.

preset_export.why: The roadmap said "turn the commit-friendly stackvo.json into a flow". Read against the code that framing is wrong: stackvo.json needs no flow — it is already in the project directory, already schema-validated, and a teammate who clones the repo already has it. What they do NOT get is the STACK: which of the twenty services are enabled and at which versions. That lives in .env, the one file nobody commits, because it is also where every password is. So the clone succeeds, the manifest is perfect, and the project still will not start until somebody says "you need MySQL 8.0, Redis and Elasticsearch on". That sentence is the preset.
preset_export.notes: A preset can never carry a secret, and that is enforced by construction rather than by filtering. `services` entries hold `enabled` and `version` — two named fields, not a passthrough map — so there is no code path by which SERVICE_MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD reaches one; it is not that a filter drops it, it is that there is nowhere to put it. `settings` is an ALLOW-LIST of five global keys, not a deny-list: Env::is_secret matches on suffix, so a key added upstream tomorrow called SERVICE_FOO_APIKEY would sail through a deny-list. An allow-list fails closed against a file this app does not own. Disabled services are included too — a preset listing only what is on cannot express "and turn Elasticsearch off", which is half of what makes two machines match. Ports and paths are excluded on purpose: they are properties of one developer's machine, and importing somebody else's is how two people end up fighting over 3306.

preset_save.notes: Pretty-printed, because the point of the file is being read in a pull request. Written atomically.

preset_plan.why: Importing a colleague's stack must never be a blind write over your own. Same shape as hosts_plan/hosts_apply and cert_plan/cert_apply — the pattern this app already uses everywhere a change leaves its own process.
preset_plan.notes: Rejections are NAMED, never silently dropped: an unknown service id, or a settings key outside the allow-list, appears in `rejected` with its reason. A preset that quietly ignores half of what it was given is how somebody concludes the feature works and then spends an afternoon on the service it skipped. Unknown ids are refused here rather than becoming a SERVICE_<JUNK>_ENABLE key in the user's .env and a compose profile that matches nothing — the failure mode CONFLICTS.md C-09 records. A file that is valid JSON but not a preset (`kind` mismatch) is an error, not a plan with zero changes: pointing the importer at a package.json has to say so rather than look successful. A preset from a NEWER version is refused rather than half-read.

preset_apply.notes: Re-plans from the file rather than trusting a plan the frontend hands back: between the review and the click, .env may have been changed by a service toggle in another pane, and writing a stale diff would silently undo it. Writes through env_writer, which backs the file up, preserves comments and ordering, and serialises against the other .env writers. `needsRegenerate` says what has to happen next — enabling a service changes what the generator emits, so the change is not live until regenerate-then-up.

php_ini_status.why: Every competitor exposes memory_limit and upload_max_filesize; StackVo could not, because .stackvo/php.ini was documented but never real — docs/*/configuration/project.md lists it and the old web UI's DockerService.js:388 lists it, but `php.ini` appears NOWHERE in core/cli. No generator mounted it, so dropping the file in did nothing. The mount had to exist before a form was worth building.
php_ini_status.notes: Three states kept apart, like Xdebug's. `exists` is the file on disk. `mounted` is read from the RUNNING container, never inferred — `stackvo up` from the Bash CLI layers three compose files, not five, and will recreate the container without the mount; None means nothing is running. `needsRecreate` is the two disagreeing. PHP reads its ini at process start, so editing a value in the bind-mounted file changes nothing until the container restarts — which is a third thing again, and the reason none of this is one boolean.

php_ini_set.why: The half of P1-9 that was cut on evidence: `memory_limit` and `upload_max_filesize` are not manifest keys and cannot become them (the schema is additionalProperties: false), and the file the docs pointed at was mounted by nothing.
php_ini_set.notes: `null` removes a directive rather than setting it to PHP's default — this file is an override layer, and leaving `memory_limit = 128M` behind because it matches today's default would keep overriding a php.ini the user may later change underneath it. Removing the last directive removes the FILE, so the mount goes with it on the next compose invocation. Comments, order and directives this app does not manage survive a patch untouched; the file is the user's and safe to commit. Values are format-checked before they are written, because PHP does not fail loudly on a malformed directive — it warns to a log nobody is watching and keeps the old value, which presents as "the setting did nothing".

project_dockerfile_preview.why: Runs the Rust generator port alongside the Bash one so its output can be compared before it replaces anything. `matchesBashOutput` is the differential check, live against the user's own projects rather than only against fixtures.
project_dockerfile_preview.notes: Strict mode is the behaviour change made visible: where Bash silently drops an incompatible extension, this refuses and names it. `skipped` always reports what compat mode would have dropped, so the difference is legible either way.

generator_verify.why: The migration gate. A fixture suite only covers the cases someone thought to write down; this renders every generated file with the Rust port against the user's real projects and real .env, so a divergence surfaces on their machine before anything depends on it.
generator_verify.notes: Reads only — it never writes a generated file. `readyToTakeOver` is true when every file matches byte-for-byte.

generate_with.why: Was the staged handover: Bash ran in every mode and `rust` refused to write on any byte difference. The takeover completed at 28/28 files identical on real data, the Bash engine was retired, and the Rust generator is the only writer.
generate_with.notes: Kept for headless callers; the UI's engine selector is gone because there is no longer an engine to select. `verify` survives as a drift check — does the disk still hold what the generator would write — which catches hand-edited generated files. generate_run is the plain write path.

events._note: Names are preserved from Socket.io so the Vue listeners keep working, with ONE deliberate change: the terminal events move from dash to colon separators for consistency. That is a 4-line change in the terminal component.

app:close_requested.notes: The window was asked to close and closeBehaviour is "ask". Rust prevents the close and emits this; the front end shows the choice dialog and answers with window_close_action.
